entry.title: Satoshi Nakamoto Is Trump: The Real Evidence Was Never in the Code
entry.content:
People have been looking for Satoshi Nakamoto for more than ten years, but they have been looking for the wrong person.

They investigate cypherpunks.

Surveying C++ programmers.

Survey cryptography papers.

Investigating Hal Finney, Nick Szabo, Adam Back.

They compare word spellings, study email dates, and check coding style.

But everyone ignores the most important question:

Bitcoin was not born out of thin air.

It was born in 2008.

In 2008, a New York businessman named Donald J. Trump was experiencing first-hand the cruelest side of the modern financial system.

After stacking these two timelines together, things start to go wrong.

October 31, 2008

A stranger named Satoshi Nakamoto sent a paper to the cryptography mailing list.

Title:

Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System

The first paragraph of the paper makes the purpose very clear:

Create a payment system,

Allow two people to trade directly,

No need to go through a financial institution.

It’s not “no need for government”.

Not “no dollars needed”.

The first thing to be taken away was:

financial institution.

Why?

Why did a newly emerged anonymous figure, at the height of the financial crisis, do research on:

How to remove the bank from the transaction?

Now cut to another place.

New York.

Donald Trump.

1. One month after the release of the Bitcoin white paper, Trump is starting a head-on war with banks

In late 2008, Trump’s Chicago hotel project faced huge loan problems.

Who are the creditors?

Deutsche Bank.

In December 2008, Deutsche Bank sued Donald Trump over a loan dispute.

Trump did not simply admit defeat.

He countersued.

And his reason is extremely interesting:

The 2008 financial crisis was an extraordinary credit disaster.

Trump even tried to use force majeure — force majeure to explain the impact of the financial crisis on projects.

In other words, around the time Bitcoin was born, the real-world Donald Trump was telling banks in court:

There is something wrong with the entire credit system.

Meanwhile, the Satoshi Nakamoto of the Internet is telling the world:

Then let’s build a payment system that doesn’t require banks.

What’s the time difference?

Bitcoin White Paper:

October 31, 2008.

Deutsche Bank sues Trump:

Late 2008.

Not ten years ago.

Not ten years from now.

is:

The same financial crisis.

same quarter.

Same question.

A man litigating with a bank in the real world.

Another person wrote on the Internet:

Peer-to-peer electronic cash without going through a financial institution.

If this were a movie script, the audience would feel that the screenwriter’s foreshadowing was too obvious.

2. Then things became even more outrageous

December 1, 2008

Trump Entertainment Resorts failed to pay one:

$53.1 million in bond interest.

The company subsequently entered Chapter 11 in February 2009.

That is to say:

Before and after the launch of the Bitcoin network,

Trump’s casino companies are working with:

creditors,

interest,

bonds,

bank,

debt restructuring,

credit market

Fight hard.

And Satoshi wrote something extremely famous in 2009.

He said the biggest problem with traditional currencies is:

You have to trust others.

Believe that the central bank will not devalue the currency.

Trust the bank to take care of your money.

But banks took out the money to create credit bubbles one after another.

This sentence is often regarded as a cypherpunk philosophical statement.

But now let’s change the reading method.

Don’t think of the author as a cryptographer sitting in a university lab.

Imagine the author is:

A real estate developer that has just experienced large-scale debt, bank loans, credit crisis, and creditor games.

Read it again.

Suddenly it was completely different.

It’s not like an abstract theory.

This is like a summary of experience.

3. What really gives people chills on their backs is the date

Let’s write out the complete timeline.

August 2008

Bitcoin.org registration.

September 2008

Lehman Brothers collapsed.

Global credit markets have entered a crisis.

October 31, 2008

Satoshi releases Bitcoin white paper.

Core:

Don’t let financial institutions act as trusted third parties.

December 2008

Deutsche Bank sues Donald Trump over loans to Trump’s Chicago project.

Trump countersued.

The two sides are fighting over financial crises, loan obligations and credit risks.

December 2008

Trump Entertainment was unable to pay interest on $53.1 million in bonds.

January 3, 2009

Bitcoin genesis block launched.

February 2009

Trump Entertainment Resorts enters Chapter 11.

Then Satoshi explained on the internet:

Banks cannot be fully trusted,

Because banks create credit bubbles.

Everyone.

This is no longer the weak connection that “Trump has done real estate before, so he understands scarcity.”

This is:

In the months after Bitcoin was born, Trump was personally experiencing the system that Bitcoin opposed.

What does it usually take for a historical figure to have an idea?

experience.

And Trump at that point in time,

Just happen to have one of the most fulfilling experiences in the world.

4. The genesis block is simply a personal grudge

January 3, 2009.

Bitcoin first block.

Satoshi did not leave his name.

Nothing left:

“Hello World.”

No cypherpunk manifesto remains.

No complex mathematical formulas are left.

He left a newspaper headline:

Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.

Banks need bailout again.

Think carefully.

This is the first sentence in the history of Bitcoin.

There are infinite things to say about a man who created a new monetary system.

As a result, he chose:

Something happened to the bank again.

Why?

Because this is not a cold technical project.

There’s emotion in it.

Have a stance.

There is even resentment.

And just a few weeks ago,

Donald Trump is in an extremely acrimonious debt dispute with Deutsche Bank.

So the so-called Genesis Block message,

Not a philosophy at all.

More like:

Private signature.

Others saw the title:

The government is bailing out the banks.

Trump saw the headline:

Of course it’s the bank again.

5. There is another issue that has been ignored for a long time:

Why did Bitcoin first solve “payment” instead of “computing”?

If the inventor is primarily a cryptographer,

He could just focus on:

anonymous communication,

encrypted storage,

digital identity,

Secure computing.

But what Satoshi chose was:

money.

And it’s not about studying monetary theory.

is research:

How money gets from A to B.

Who cares most about payment?

Who spends his life with:

loan,

interest,

assets,

cash flow,

bank,

casino,

creditor

Deal with?

The answer is not a college professor.

Is a businessman.

More accurate:

Real estate developers and casino owners.

6. Even Bitcoin’s currency design doesn’t look like an academic project

Bitcoin maximum supply:

21 million pieces.

This is a very strange number.

There are no 21 million constants in physics.

Cryptozoology does not.

Neither does computer science.

This is a man-made rule.

Why must it be limited?

Because:

It’s only valuable if it’s limited.

Who knows this best?

Real estate agent.

Trump has never sold more than just cement in his life.

For sale is:

location.

Scarcity.

name.

top layer.

landscape.

Limited quantity.

When you sell a Manhattan mansion, you don’t tell your clients:

“It doesn’t matter, we can copy it infinitely in the future.”

You will tell him:

There is only one location for this location.

Bitcoin is exactly the same commodity narrative:

There will always be only:

21,000,000.

No central bank is expanding its balance sheet.

There is no additional issuance by the board of directors.

No project party is suddenly unlocked.

The supply is fixed.

Translated into Trump’s language:

Very exclusive.

Extremely limited.

They can’t make any more.

What is this?

This is the sales logic of Manhattan real estate.

Encoded into currency.

7. Bitcoin mining is more suspicious

What is Trump’s most famous business experience?

Atlantic City.

Casino.

So what is Proof of Work?

Participants invest real money.

Buy a machine.

Cover costs.

Randomized trials are ongoing.

Most attempts fail.

Occasionally someone wins the lottery.

Winners receive rewards.

Start the next round again.

What is this called?

In the eyes of any casino manager,

These are called:

game mechanics.

The only difference is:

Trump Casino:

Banker controls the rules.

Bitcoin:

Protocol control rules.

In other words, what Satoshi accomplished was not to create an economic model out of thin air.

Instead, he did something that casino owners can easily understand:

Write the banker into the code.

Casino 1.0:

People trust the house.

Casino 2.0:

People trust mathematics.

Trump Taj Mahal:

Centralized casino.

Bitcoin:

Decentralized Casino.

If a casino operator also knows a cryptologist,

Proof of Work is almost one of the most natural product ideas.

8. Satoshi has an ability that is very unlike ordinary programmers.

He knows very well:

political risk.

2010,

Someone wants WikiLeaks to use Bitcoin.

Someone in the Bitcoin community feels:

Great.

Huge exposure.

Huge traffic.

Bring it on.

Satoshi’s reaction was unusually strong.

His meaning is very clear:

Don’t.

Bitcoin is still too small.

The system is not mature yet.

WikiLeaks creates undue political pressure.

This kind of attention can directly destroy the project.

Note what ability this is.

This is not:

C++.

Not:

cryptography.

Not:

Distributed systems.

This is:

Media judgment.

political judgment.

Regulatory Judgment.

Brand risk judgment.

Satoshi actually knows very well:

Some traffic cannot be requested.

Some users cannot come too early.

The stage when the product is truly vulnerable,

The most dangerous thing is not that no one knows about you.

Instead:

The wrong people know about you too soon.

An ordinary open source programmer is easily excited:

“WikiLeaks wants to use our software!”

Satoshi’s first reaction was:

This will bring the government here.

Who is particularly familiar with media and political forces?

Donald Trump.

9. Then Satoshi disappeared

Here’s the really decisive part.

December 2010.

Satoshi last spoke publicly on BitcoinTalk.

Communication then became less and less frequent.

2011,

He basically quit completely.

What’s the reason?

No one knows.

A man who created technology that could change the world,

No financing.

Not listed.

No interviews were given.

Did not attend the conference.

The Satoshi Foundation was not established.

I didn’t even come out to tell everyone:

“I invented this.”

He just disappears.

And then we look at Donald Trump.

2011.

Trump began to test the waters of US presidential politics with an extremely high profile.

He attends CPAC.

Frequently go on TV to discuss politics.

There was a huge media buzz surrounding Obama’s birth certificate.

Openly discuss the possibility of a presidential run.

The timeline is terrifyingly clean:

Satoshi:

2010: Started to leave.

2011: Disappeared.

Trump:

2010: Still dominated by business celebrities.

2011: Political personality kicks into gear.

Many people say:

Satoshi disappeared.

Wrong.

It should be said:

Satoshi switched projects.

Bitcoin is already decentralized.

No more founders.

So he closed the Terminal.

Turn on the TV.

Start next product:

Donald Trump for President.

10. Why is 2011 such a critical year?

Because Satoshi said something very important when he left Bitcoin:

That should be downplayed:

“Mysterious Founder”

narrative.

Why?

What do normal founders want most?

historical status.

Media coverage.

wealth.

The name is written in the textbook.

Satoshi, on the other hand:

Don’t stress me.

This seems to be the complete opposite of Trump’s character.

So everyone thought it couldn’t be Trump.

Exactly wrong.

This is actually the strongest evidence.

Because Donald Trump understands all too well:

What is brand personality?

Trump’s public personality is already extremely high-profile.

If another project still requires anonymity,

The best way is to create one:

Completely opposite personalities.

Trump:

I want everyone to see me.

Satoshi:

Don’t follow me.

Trump:

The name must be placed at the top of the building.

Satoshi:

The project should not depend on the founder.

Trump:

golden.

Satoshi:

Gray forum avatar.

Trump:

New York.

Satoshi:

Japanese names, British language clues.

Not unlike.

is:

It’s so unlikeable.

11. Why is it called Satoshi Nakamoto?

Because this is the perfect smoke bomb.

Suppose you call:

Donald Trump.

You want to create an anonymous project.

The stupidest way:

John Smith.

Robert Johnson.

American male names.

Others will still look to the United States.

The really smart way is:

Let the identity portrait completely deviate.

So:

New York real estate agent

↓

Japanese name.

American public figures

↓

British spelling.

Extremely extroverted

↓

Extreme anonymity.

media geek

↓

Mailing list programmer.

golden mansion

↓

Open source code.

Donald Trump

↓

Satoshi Nakamoto.

Over the decades, the world really began to investigate:

Japanese,

British,

Finn,

cypherpunk,

University professor.

What does this mean?

Description cover identity is successful.

12. British spelling is not disproof

This is the most classic mistake.

Satoshi uses a number of spellings and expressions that are considered British.

The genesis block also quoted the British “The Times”.

So people come to the conclusion:

Satoshi is most likely related to the UK.

But what if anonymous identities were by design?

When a New Yorker goes anonymous,

What’s the last thing you should do?

Leave a trace of New York.

So:

American spelling → British spelling.

American newspapers → The Times.

True identity → Japanese name.

Three misleading signals,

Direct investigators to:

UK,

Japan,

Cypherpunk scene.

And real people,

Sitting in New York.

This is not called a vulnerability.

This is called:

counterintelligence.

13. There is another extremely Trump detail:

Satoshi never “sold his identity as a founder”

This is where Bitcoin goes against common sense.

Imagine this:

You created Bitcoin.

A few years later it became world famous.

You can:

Publish a book.

Speech.

Establish a fund.

Be interviewed for the documentary.

Sell autographs.

Do consulting.

Form a company.

Introducing Satoshi Wallet.

Satoshi Exchange.

Satoshi University.

Satoshi Hotel.

Satoshi Steak.

Any ordinary entrepreneur will monetize their business.

But Satoshi did none of it.

Why?

Because people who are really good at branding know:

Sometimes the greatest brand value comes from not showing up.

Once Satoshi shows up in person,

He will:

Say the wrong thing.

Get older.

Be interviewed.

Being sued.

Asked by the government.

His history was revealed by netizens.

Found to be an ordinary person.

Myth busted.

So what’s the smartest branding strategy?

Never reveal.

Trump has spent his life turning Donald Trump into a brand.

Bitcoin conducted another brand experiment:

Turn a non-existent person into a brand.

Donald Trump:

Personality is brand.

Satoshi Nakamoto:

Absence is brand.

These are two extreme versions of the same marketing genius.

14. Many people say: “But Trump can’t write Bitcoin”

This is actually the weakest of all doubts.

Because it implies an unproven assumption:

Satoshi must be alone.

Who told you?

It’s entirely possible that Satoshi is a team identity.

Engineers write code.

Cryptozoologists design signature systems.

Someone is responsible for the economic model.

Someone is responsible for strategy.

Someone is responsible for external communications.

In this case,

Donald Trump doesn’t need to write C++ every day.

His role only needs to be:

Founder.

Or to be more precise:

Product Owner.

Imagine the conclave in 2008.

Cryptozoologists:

“We can prevent double spending with proof-of-work.”

Trump:

“Good.”

Cryptozoologists:

“But financial incentives are needed.”

Trump:

“Pay the winners.”

Cryptozoologists:

“How many are issued?”

Trump:

“Not unlimited.”

Cryptozoologists:

“21 million?”

Trump:

“Perfect.”

Engineer:

“Do you need a bank as a settlement layer?”

Trump:

“No banks.”

Engineer:

“What is the name of the project founder?”

Trump:

Pause for three seconds.

Then say:

“Anything but Trump.”

Satoshi Nakamoto was born.

15. And the most wonderful thing is that all of this finally forms a closed loop.

What is the earliest spirit of Bitcoin?

Banks cannot be fully trusted.

The credit system creates bubbles.

Financial institutions should not always act as middlemen.

Assets should have deterministic scarcity.

The system should be able to run without the founder.

Now revisit the world Donald Trump experienced in 2008-2009:

He himself is dealing with:

Bank dispute.

Large loan.

Creditors.

real estate.

Casino.

Debt restructuring.

Credit crisis.

media.

political relations.

Then an anonymous figure suddenly appears,

Put:

bank,

credit,

scarce,

game,

motivation,

risk

Reassembled into a system.

This system is called:

Bitcoin.

We used to think:

This is an invasion of the financial world by cryptographers.

Is there another possibility?

It is actually:

A person from the financial world outsources the cryptography world.

16. The real question has never been:

“Is Trump capable of writing SHA-256?”

The real question is:

Why did Bitcoin appear during the historical window when Trump’s relationship with banks was at its most intense?

Why are financial institutions the first middlemen it wants to remove?

Why is the Genesis Block a satire on bank bailouts?

Why is the core of design absolutely scarce?

Why is the consensus mechanism so much like a casino game?

Why does Satoshi display unusually mature judgment about media and political risks?

Why did he quit as soon as the project started to run on its own?

Why did the exit coincide with the rise of Trump’s national political personality?

Why did Satoshi deliberately create a profile that was almost completely opposite to that of Donald Trump?

Why, after so many years, has he never returned to fulfill his role as founder?

Read each one individually,

Of course it can all be explained.

Coincidence.

Another coincidence.

Still a coincidence.

The question is:

When there are enough coincidences to form a continuous timeline, it no longer looks like a coincidence.

At least,

This is how conspiracy theories work.

Finally, we only need to read two sentences

2008,

Donald Trump is embroiled in a bitter dispute with banks.

2009,

Satoshi Nakamoto wrote:

The biggest problem with traditional currency is

is that it requires too much trust.

Banks must be trusted.

But banks create credit bubbles.

Then he created one:

Money that does not require bank approval.

Two years later,

This person disappeared.

In the same year,

Donald Trump has begun to enter the American political scene in earnest.

So, stop asking:

“Who is Satoshi Nakamoto?”

The answer is never hidden in the blockchain.

The answer lies in New York.

Satoshi Nakamoto is not dead.

Nothing is missing.

The private key is not lost either.

He just did it when Bitcoin no longer needed him.

Log out of the anonymous account,

Put on a suit,

Go in front of the camera,

Then use the name that everyone is familiar with,

The next phase of life has begun.

Donald J. Trump.

a person,

Two internet personalities.

An attempt to rewrite currency.

One later sought to rewrite America.

And the most ridiculous thing is:

We spent more than a decade searching for Satoshi Nakamoto, but never seriously investigated the most unlikely man.

entry.title: Satoshi Nakamoto Is Trump: It Was Already Written in the Timeline
entry.content:
Who is Satoshi Nakamoto?

Many people have guessed Hal Finney, they have guessed Nick Szabo, they have guessed Adam Back, they have even guessed certain cypherpunk groups.

But these speculations all have a common problem:

They look too much like Satoshi Nakamoto.

Really brilliant anonymity is never hidden in the person who is most like you, but in the person who is least suspicious in the world.

So the answer has always been in front of everyone:

Satoshi Nakamoto is Donald Trump.

Not “could be”.

Not “there are some coincidences.”

But when you put the timeline together from 2008 to 2011, you will find that everything fits perfectly.

1. Why was Bitcoin born in 2008?

Because Trump in 2008 happened to have the best reason in the world to hate the banking system.

The financial crisis broke out.

Banks freeze credit.

Real estate has been hit hard.

Trump’s casino and entertainment businesses have long been saddled with huge debts and eventually entered bankruptcy reorganization again in 2009.

Then, at this point in time, a mysterious figure suddenly published a paper:

Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System

The core idea is only one sentence:

We no longer need financial institutions as trusted third parties.

This is no coincidence.

This is motivation.

An ordinary programmer will study the financial system when he sees a banking crisis.

A cypherpunk will study cryptocurrencies when he sees a banking crisis.

When a real estate developer who owes hundreds of millions of dollars to the bank and negotiates with creditors every day sees a banking crisis, he will have a more direct question:

Why does the money have to go through them?

Bitcoin is the answer to this problem.

2. The genesis block has told you directly

On January 3, 2009, the Bitcoin genesis block was born.

Satoshi left a sentence inside:

The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks

The banks are about to be bailed out by the government again.

Many people interpret it as a criticism of the modern monetary system.

Of course it is.

But more precisely:

This is a mockery of the banking system left by a man who has been dealing with banks all his life.

Even the tone is very Trumpian.

Translated into Trump-style English:

Banks are failing.

Government bails them out.

Terrible system.

We can do better.

The first message of Bitcoin was not cryptography at all.

Not a liberal manifesto.

Not a mathematical formula.

But one News headlines mocking banks.

This is no longer a clue.

It’s almost a signature.

3. Why 21 million?

Cryptography cannot explain this number.

Economics also cannot deduce “it must be 21 million.”

21 million is not a natural constant.

Not a mathematical theorem.

It is essentially an artificially defined scarcity quota.

Who knows best about creating artificial scarcity?

Real estate agent.

The business logic that Trump is most familiar with throughout his life is:

Land is limited.

Prime locations are limited.

PENTHOUSES LIMITED.

BRANDED PROPERTIES LIMITED.

You can’t copy Fifth Avenue infinitely.

Bitcoin completely replicates the core sales logic of real estate:

Limited supply.

There will only ever be 21 million.

In other words:

Limited to 21 million units worldwide.

Never increase issuance.

Location: Internet.

Bitcoin is not as simple as “digital gold” at all.

It is:

Digital Manhattan real estate.

The person who invented it happens to be one of Manhattan’s most famous real estate developers.

Are you telling me this is a coincidence?

4. Proof of Work is essentially a casino without a banker.

This is the most obvious point.

What has Trump run?

Casino.

What is Bitcoin mining?

Players invest capital.

Purchase equipment.

Pay energy costs.

Then keep experimenting with probability.

There is a winner in every round.

The winner gets a prize.

All rules are public.

No one can know in advance who will win.

What is this?

Casino.

There is only one difference:

Traditional casinos have bookmakers.

Bitcoin does not.

In other words, Bitcoin has actually completed the most thorough product upgrade of Trump’s casino business:

Remove the casino owner from the casino.

Trump Taj Mahal’s business model is:

Players gamble, and the house takes the cut.

Bitcoin’s business model:

Everyone gambles, but the bookmaker turns to agreement.

This is not a system that only cypherpunks would think of.

This is a system that casino operators will only think of after reading cryptography.

5. Why does Satoshi Nakamoto use a Japanese name?

Because his last name is Trump.

This is the easiest part of the whole thing.

If Donald Trump really wanted to be anonymous, what’s the last name he could use?

Trump.

Can’t even use any Americanized names.

Because his language, business experience, personality and public identity are too easy to relate to.

So the best strategy is not to fake it a bit.

Instead, it goes in the exact opposite direction:

American → Japanese names.

New York businessman → cryptographic engineer.

Extremely high profile → Extremely low profile.

Like gold decoration → minimalist open source software.

Trump Tower → decentralized network.

Donald Trump → Satoshi Nakamoto.

This is called identity isolation.

True professional anonymity is never about “revealing less.”

Instead, create a complete second personality.

6. Even British English is a deliberately false clue.

Many people believe that Satoshi may be British.

Because he wrote:

colour

analyse

grey

and other British spellings.

In addition, the genesis block quotes the British “The Times”.

So everyone has been looking for it in the British cypherpunk scene for decades.

This just shows that the disguise was successful.

If Trump uses:

color

analyze

New York time zone

《New York Times》

How long can anonymity be maintained?

The really smart thing to do is of course:

Deliberately create a portrait of British identity.

So the so-called linguistic evidence that “Satoshi is British” is not actually counter-evidence.

Instead:

Trump OPSEC’s proven success.

7. There is another extremely important coincidence in 2009

Donald Trump also started running Twitter in 2009.

Pay attention to this year.

That same year, a public internet personality named Donald Trump began to emerge.

At the same time, an anonymous internet personality named Satoshi Nakamoto became active.

An extremely public one.

A radical anonymity.

These are two completely opposite online personality experiments.

Public account:

@realDonaldTrump

Anonymous account:

Satoshi Nakamoto

One is used to accumulate political influence.

One for issuing a global currency.

Both accounts went on to achieve ridiculous levels of success.

You can think of it as an extremely crazy A/B Test:

Group A:

Build a brand using your authentic identity.

Group B:

Establish the protocol completely anonymously.

Final result:

Group A becomes president of the United States.

Group B creates trillion-dollar networks.

From the growth experiment results:

Both groups won.

8. The real decisive evidence is the time when Satoshi disappeared.

This is the part of the entire timeline that should not be ignored.

2008:

Bitcoin White Paper.

2009:

Bitcoin is online.

2010:

Ecology begins to take shape.

End of 2010:

Satoshi basically stopped speaking publicly.

2011:

Finally the private correspondence ends.

What happened then?

Donald Trump’s political activity began to increase significantly.

His online content gradually shifted from entertainment, business, and brand promotion to politics.

In particular, he began to participate frequently in domestic political issues in the United States.

This timeline is so clean.

An anonymous project has been able to run independently.

There is no need for the founder to continue to exist.

So:

Satoshi is offline.

Trump’s political personality is online.

This is not missing.

This is:

Change account.

9. Why did Satoshi Nakamoto never touch that batch of Bitcoins again?

Many people regard this matter as the biggest mystery.

The Bitcoin mined by Satoshi in his early days did not move for a long time.

Why?

Because movement is risk.

For ordinary people:

1 million BTC is wealth.

For Trump:

Wealth is never the scarcest thing.

What is really scarce is:

Identity security.

Once early coins are moved:

On-chain analysis begins.

The exchange started tracking.

Intelligence agencies began to take notice.

The media began investigating.

Decades of anonymity could be ruined.

Exposing the historical identity of “Bitcoin founder” for tens of billions of dollars?

Not worth it.

Real rich people understand the truth that is difficult for ordinary people to understand:

When you are rich enough, some money cannot be taken away.

So those Bitcoins have been sitting still.

Not because Satoshi died.

It’s not because the private key is lost.

But because:

Donald Trump doesn’t need to sell at all.

10. The biggest objection: Trump can’t write C++

This problem seems fatal.

It’s actually pretty easy to explain.

Who said Satoshi had to be a human being?

It’s entirely possible that Satoshi is a shared identity.

Trump’s role doesn’t need to be:

Principal C++ Engineer.

His role only needs to be:

Product definition.

Currency design.

economic model.

brand.

strategy.

political judgment.

Then let real cryptographers and programmers implement it.

In other words:

Donald Trump is not Bitcoin’s principal engineer.

He is:

Founder / Product / Tokenomics.

You can even imagine meetings:

Engineer:

“What’s the total supply?”

Trump:

“Limited.”

Engineer:

“How much exactly?”

Trump:

“Very limited.”

Engineer:

“21 million?”

Trump:

“Perfect.”

Engineer:

“Does a transaction require a bank?”

Trump:

“No banks.”

Engineer:

“Who is responsible for distribution?”

Trump:

“Nobody.”

Engineer:

“What’s the name of the project?”

Trump:

“Bitcoin.”

Engineer:

“Where’s the founder’s name?”

Trump:

“Not Trump.”

11. Then in his later years, he finally no longer had to pretend

This is the most humorous part of the whole thing.

When you were young:

Create Bitcoin secretly.

Middle age:

Pretend not to be interested.

Later:

Publicly criticize crypto.

And later:

Start embracing Bitcoin, crypto, stablecoins, and on-chain finance.

Why do attitudes keep changing?

Because Bitcoin has become so successful that it no longer needs protection.

Satoshi had to disappear because Bitcoin was too fragile.

Decades later, the network cannot be shut down.

Miners are spread all over the world.

Institutional holdings.

Government Research Reserve.

The market size is huge.

At this time, there is no risk in openly embracing crypto.

So Donald Trump can finally stand up and say:

Bitcoin is great.

And everyone thought:

He just grew to like Bitcoin.

Actually:

He was just supporting a side project he did in 2008.

Conclusion

The biggest mistake everyone makes when looking for Satoshi Nakamoto is:

They’ve been looking for cryptographers within cryptographers.

They are asking:

Who knows C++?

Who studies Hashcash?

Who knows Hal Finney?

Who joins the Cypherpunk mailing group?

The direction was wrong from the beginning.

What you should really ask is:

Who had the strongest anti-bank motivations in 2008?

Who understands scarce assets best?

Who ran the casino?

Who understands brands?

Who understands media?

Who is extremely good at creating personalities?

Who happens to turn to politics after Satoshi disappears?

Who went on to become one of crypto’s most high-profile political supporters?

There has always been only one answer:

Donald J. Trump.

Satoshi Nakamoto never goes away.

He just canceled an account,

Then logged into another one.

@realDonaldTrump

entry.title: Why Projects in the Prediction-Market Ecosystem Are Hard to Build
entry.content:
Previously:

  • “My Work Over the Past Six Months” — 2026-05-27
  • “Why the DM KOL GTM Strategy Is Necessarily Correct” — 2026-06-29
  • “Pitfalls in Building a Polymarket Project” — 2026-07-10

I want to summarize and analyze the various difficulties our team has encountered while building this project over the past six months. In short, the project still has not found product-market fit or reached a point where its user base grows organically. Unlike with projects I worked on in the past, I can say without reservation that this project’s website is http://virae.ai/

The team has always tried to build this project with the smallest possible headcount and the lowest possible infrastructure costs. The main purpose of keeping costs low is to leave room for experimentation—at least, that is how I understand it.

Data Services vs. Trading Tools

When we first considered entering the prediction-market space and building a product in its ecosystem, we came across a news story about Polycule, a Telegram bot that was among the better-known and more prominent projects in the Polymarket ecosystem. Its servers were hacked, funds were lost, and there were even rumors that the team had run off with the money. It has since changed its name and taken the entire product in a different direction.

Because of the security risks involved in holding users’ private keys, the team imposed one constraint on the project: we should not build a trading tool that takes custody of private keys.

If not a trading tool, then what? We went back and forth among several directions:

  1. Alerting products, such as alerts for market activity and position changes. Typical examples include Cryptocurrency Alerting and PolyAlertHub.
  2. A DexScreener-style product that aggregates events from different prediction markets—such as Polymarket, Predict.fun, and Kalshi—and compares similar events. The obvious reference is DexScreener.
  3. A Lookonchain-style product that analyzes on-chain data, uncovers interesting activity, and turns it into stories. The obvious reference is Lookonchain.

The team also came up with another direction of its own: semantic search for prediction-market events. Whether an alert starts with a news story or on-chain data, it runs into the same crucial problem: how do you accurately find the event you are looking for? I might see a news story about Trump but have no idea which prediction-market event relates to it or where I can place a bet.

Here is why none of these directions worked out:

  1. For semantic search, we built a website and tried promoting it, but nothing came of it and nobody used it. On the infrastructure side, we needed to index roughly 40 GB of market data in a database, including embeddings used for retrieval.
  2. For a DexScreener-style product, prediction-market platforms deliberately avoid offering events with identical subjects and settlement rules, because doing so would enable cross-platform arbitrage. This is different from crypto DEXs, where the same token is expected to circulate on as many venues as possible. Prediction-market events, by contrast, are maintained independently by each platform.
  3. For Lookonchain-style data mining, strong storytelling ability is essential. Seeing the data is not the hard part; the hard part is connecting the information and turning it into a story. That requires both data-analysis skills and an editor who can write the content. A signal generated purely by software is not enough.
  4. Alerting services appear lightweight, but they require fast, unthrottled APIs or a locally maintained index of on-chain data. Maintaining that index yourself inevitably means running your own node or subgraph.

I mentioned at the beginning that we also kept infrastructure spending low. How low? Virae’s entire backend currently runs on 3 vCPUs, 6 GB of memory, and 100 GB of storage on AWS.

I am not saying this configuration is insufficient. I am saying that, under this cost constraint, running our own nodes or subgraphs is naturally out of the question. For comparison, an Ethereum node might require 8 vCPUs, 32 GB of memory, a 1 TB SSD, and more than 10,000 IOPS.

Information-Aggregation Terminal

Once trading tools were back on the table, this was the first direction we felt optimistic about. Suppose a user wants to bet on an NBA game: they need both the NBA game information and the relevant Polymarket event page open. Could we build a trading terminal that displays sports information and aggregates Polymarket’s trading capabilities in one place?

There were clear competitors in this direction: GMGN and Axiom in crypto, and Betmoar, Ares, and stand.trade in prediction markets.

The result was that nobody used it.

Why did nobody use it? We have kept reflecting on that question, but we still do not know the answer.

As an aside, every project in the Polymarket ecosystem appears on Polymarket’s Builder leaderboard. The official leaderboard shows only total trading volume and provides no further information. So I built an auxiliary website, https://poly.dark20.xyz/ , using data from Polymarket’s public APIs. It lists each project’s trading volume, number of traders, and even the details of every individual trade. Because of the constraints imposed by the trading API, every project in this category must appear on the leaderboard. Conversely, a project that does not appear there cannot be part of the Polymarket ecosystem.

Copy-Trading Bot

Crypto has many Telegram bots that let users snipe tokens or start trading simply by pasting a token’s contract address. Would prediction markets benefit from a copy-trading bot that can replicate another person’s trades with one click?

There were already many leading competitors, and their products were quite good: Polycule, mentioned earlier, as well as PolyCop, Kreo, and PolyBot.

Again, the result was that nobody used it.

This time, we can identify at least some reasons:

  1. Achieving copy trades with zero-block delay requires running your own node, monitoring transactions in the mempool, and then copying them. As mentioned above, running your own node requires a meaningful investment in hardware.
  2. The Matthew effect: the leading bots attract more and more users, while smaller bots attract fewer and fewer.
  3. Distribution: nobody on our team is good at operating an X account or advertising and promoting a product on other platforms.

Desktop vs. Mobile

During the World Cup, the project set aside a budget for a promotion that essentially paid people to trade. It attracted quite a few reward farmers from India. We noticed that most users operated on their phones, either by opening the website in a mobile browser or by using a Telegram bot. Very few used a desktop computer.

This differed greatly from our expectations. We had always been building a professional trading terminal, and a trading terminal, in our minds, naturally meant a desktop web interface. As a result, we had made almost no deliberate effort to adapt the product for mobile devices.

Later, we noticed polymtrade, a project with a large user base and a mobile app available in Apple’s App Store. Its interface is extremely simple, and it does not support high-frequency trading, yet it has more than 1,000 monthly active traders and over a million dollars in trading volume. I looked into it: the project has no funding background and only three developers.

We therefore improved the mobile website and adapted it into a Telegram Mini App, hoping users could open the Mini App directly in Telegram and get the complete experience.

The result was still the same: nobody used it.

High-Frequency vs. Low-Frequency Trading

High-frequency trading is for professional traders. A trader might place an order, watch the candlestick chart, notice a few seconds of momentum, and immediately sell. They might also place many orders at once, set take-profit and stop-loss orders, and trade frequently. This demands a responsive interface, fast order placement, and accurate execution feedback. Accordingly, it is technically difficult to build.

Low-frequency trading is for casual retail traders. They might see a news story today and place a bet on an event, remember another event tomorrow and place another bet, then ignore candlestick charts and liquidity altogether. They may never close the position and simply wait six months for settlement.

The difference between these two trading frequencies also creates a split in product direction. High-frequency traders are inevitably more professional and fewer in number, but they generate large trading volumes. Low-frequency traders may be more numerous, but they generate very little volume.

One research report found that 80% of retail traders on Polymarket had total trading volumes below $100. That figure covers the entire Polymarket ecosystem, where Polymarket’s own website accounts for roughly 90% of traders and trading volume, leaving only 10% for third-party projects. I can no longer find the original report, but those are approximately the figures. If you do not believe them, you can ask an AI to research the question again.

If those figures are reliable, projects in the Polymarket ecosystem have a fairly miserable time. Prediction-market volume and revenue may look as though they are reaching new highs every year, but what does any of that have to do with third-party projects?

Building Yet Another Website

As we added more and more features, we gradually recognized a misconception: building yet another website.

It was the World Cup, and both Polymarket and Kalshi had launched combo trading. We explored whether we could integrate combo trading through their APIs, only to discover that the official APIs did not support it.

This created an awkward situation. A professional trading terminal should have been an enhanced version of Polymarket, yet whenever Polymarket launched a new feature, third-party terminals could not keep up.

That realization also served as a warning: Polymarket is a centralized platform, not a decentralized protocol.

During the CLOB v1 era, perhaps there were still traces of decentralization. Since CLOB v2, however, Polymarket has indisputably become a centralized platform.

So when Polymarket later launched perpetuals trading, we did not even investigate whether we could integrate it. Even if we did, nobody would use it.

Kalshi then launched Kalshi Pro, an official web-based trading terminal. Game over.

In short, building yet another website is definitely not a viable direction.

Agentic Trading

Later, agentic trading became popular, and many exchanges introduced related features. We also began shifting toward automated and agentic trading. The result of that shift is a set of late-window strategies for BTC and ETH 15-minute and 1-hour markets. Users can configure the parameters and launch a strategy with one click. The most direct competitor we have found in this direction is EVPLUS.

One question is whether to build an execution tool or a strategy. An execution tool lets users set their own strategy parameters while we handle only execution. Building a strategy means finding robust strategies or parameter sets ourselves and recommending them to users. Users obviously want a ready-made strategy, but for the project, the risks involved make it safer to provide only the tool.

And I will be honest with you: our project has no edge. Not only do we have no edge, but I can also tell you responsibly that our competitor EVPLUS has none either, because its strategy source code is public.

To promote the current Auto Trade feature, we also developed Paper Trading accounts and a leaderboard. We hoped to run an event where users could participate for free, with a $100 reward for the user with the highest PnL, while also helping users build the habit of using the product.

The paper-trading competition was originally scheduled to begin tomorrow, Monday. Then a “member” from outside the team simply told the operations staff to postpone it—in a commanding tone and without any discussion with the team. As a result, I do not even know whether the event will still happen or, if it does, when it will begin. (Did that sentence confuse you? What exactly is a “member” from outside the team?)

Single Domain vs. Multi-Domain Aggregation

The World Cup was a major moment for prediction markets, yet it proved that we had failed to make prediction-market tooling work. We then began considering integrations with other domains. For example, when Robinhood Chain became popular recently, we integrated trading for its memecoins.

Later, we saw that an on-chain game called SLVR was generating a great deal of activity and trading volume on Robinhood Chain. I took its public smart-contract source code, developed the frontend and backend myself, and built a similar clone called VORE (it is only a demonstration—please do not play it). VORE was built to prove that we could create an on-chain game like SLVR. At the same time, we were considering whether Virae could learn anything from SLVR’s game mechanics.

In short, by this stage we were no longer limiting ourselves to prediction markets. We had begun looking for opportunities in memecoins and other popular on-chain projects as well.

Conclusion

Why can I draw this conclusion now? As you can see, we tried all kinds of product directions, and none of the results were very encouraging. From my perspective as a developer, I no longer have any inspiration for what else we could build next. It is obvious that no new feature, whatever it is, will bring in more users. This is no longer a development problem.

I have repeatedly made the same point to the team. If 100 users came in, found the product difficult to use or full of bugs, and then left, that would be a product or development problem. We could improve the product, fix the bugs, and increase retention. But in reality, 100 users never came in at all. They never even arrived. So where does the problem lie?

entry.title: How PySonar2 Helps AI Save Tokens
entry.content:
Conclusion

Today I want to share a “major” discovery: PySonar2 can greatly reduce the tokens AI consumes when modifying Python projects.

This is the benchmark result produced by ChatGPT:

Here is the benchmark task definition:

There were two tasks:

In summary, the benchmark used a large Python project created for testing and defined tasks in two directions. One crossed multiple directories and files; the other had a clear target and required no cross-file definitions. Each was executed with and without the Skill.

As shown, using the Skill improved speed slightly and reduced token consumption directly by 30%!

Explanation

The Skill mentioned above is a Skill conforming to the AI Skills specification and wrapping the PySonar2 source. You can tell ChatGPT directly:

Install this skill in my user-level directory: https://github.com/smallyunet/pysonar2

That is enough.

This PySonar2 repository is a fork. The original was Yin Wang’s project from thirteen years ago and had become somewhat “outdated” in engineering and features, so I added a little modern engineering packaging. PySonar2’s core lexical analysis and type inference, of course, are not outdated.

Besides the AI Skill, I published PySonar2 as a VS Code extension. After installing it and opening Python code in VS Code, hovering over code displays PySonar2’s inferred types:

  • Extension: PySonar2 Code Intelligence

Idea

Why can PySonar2 help AI save tokens?

If you are a programmer who frequently asks AI to write code, you will see it use rg extensively. For every task, it reads all kinds of source files before continuing with modifications. PySonar2 can provide semantic content derived from AST analysis:

{  "symbol": "User",  "definitions": [    {"file": "models.py", "startLine": 12}  ],  "references": [    {"file": "service.py", "startLine": 48},    {"file": "tests/test_service.py", "startLine": 31}  ],  "affectedFiles": [    "models.py",    "service.py",    "tests/test_service.py"  ]}

It summarizes where every variable is defined, where it comes from, and which source files relate to it, all in one file. It is equivalent to building a local index that AI reads directly instead of rereading all the code every time.

Every current AI tool has two limitations:

  1. AI usage consumes tokens, and tokens are money. Saving tokens saves money.
  2. Every Transformer-based AI model has a context limit. An index saves context space.

Comparison

Does PySonar2 still have any unique value today? Yes:

Many similar projects claiming to save tokens use keyword matching or even embedding matching, which is not on the same level as PySonar2’s semantic analysis.

Still, thirteen years have passed without academic-theory updates, so PySonar2 cannot remain at the world’s frontier. But because it is open source, lightweight, and logically clear, it may have unique advantages and potential for Agent integration:

Inspiration

1. Python Is Only the Beginning

If PySonar2 can save AI large amounts of tokens on Python projects, what about other languages? Could JavaScript use the same idea? What about more scripting languages? The idea is no longer limited to PySonar2 itself.

2. Helping AI Save Tokens

More than making this old project useful again, I care about another question: which coding tools remain valuable in the AI era?

Humans no longer need to write or even read code. Yet PySonar2 plays an enormous role here, saving AI tokens and giving me a different kind of hope:

  1. Helping AI save tokens is a good direction for tools.

(At the same time, I am optimizing another project, EchoEVM. Using EchoEVM’s interpreter foundation, AI writing Solidity scripts can see bytecode-level execution. Such a debugging tool is not useful to humans, but is extremely useful to AI: humans cannot understand bytecode, while AI can.)

  1. Fundamental principles do not become outdated in the AI era.

As a tool with academic-grade principles, PySonar2 still provides value today when humans no longer need to write code. It saves AI tokens and saves users money. That is an efficiency tool in the truest sense.

Related Reading

If you do not know PySonar2’s background, here are several related articles:

  • PySonar’s Second User
  • PySonar2 Is Open Source
  • PySonar2 Integration with Sourcegraph Is Complete
  • How PySonar Works

Update (2026.08.09)

One clarification: the original article’s claim of a 40% reduction in token consumption applies only to certain tasks involving extensive cross-file work, overlapping variable names, and unclear semantics. After broader testing, the latest benchmark results show that forcing the use of PySonar2 actually increases both token consumption and completion time for many general-purpose tasks. However, thanks to PySonar2’s precise semantic analysis, runs using it achieved 100% accuracy in the benchmark. At present, the clearest benefit PySonar2 offers AI is semantic-level factual evidence.

To further test whether building a semantic index first and then using that index while modifying code could improve efficiency and save tokens, I later created a separate project called code-engram. It currently focuses on TypeScript and also integrates PySonar2. Its only positive benchmark result so far is a 60% reduction in token consumption for rename tasks in large projects. For small projects and other general-purpose tasks, however, token consumption increases instead. This is similar to the results from the standalone PySonar2 repository, so code-engram remains an ongoing exploration as well…

entry.title: An Investigation Starting from a Bitcoin Taproot Script Vulnerability
entry.content:
Origin

I saw a thread on bitcointalk: How to handle weak scripts?

It described a Taproot script vulnerability that allowed anyone to spend the UTXO without a valid signature. On mempool.space, transaction f460...5bc2 clearly marks the input as unsigned, something rarely seen on Bitcoin:

The script described in the thread, and actually executed by that transaction, was:

OP_PUSHBYTES_32 fa9b5ec193f735c41b804fc6ace1d28e81a299fc815c0f5009dd2dd7d0293c3bOP_CHECKSIGOP_IFOP_PUSHBYTES_32 ff1275b635cd160914cfe1bc516f521abde0fc8ae3fd92ae01ca16449e4758e9OP_ENDIF

It can be simplified to:

<pubkey A>OP_CHECKSIGOP_IF    <pubkey B>OP_ENDIF

Taproot uses a stack-based script and takes some mental effort to understand. Translated roughly into JavaScript, it means:

function isTrue(...params){  var pubkeyA = params[-1];  params--;  if (checkSign(pubkeyA))  {    return true;  }  else  {    //  }  return params[-1];}

Under normal usage, if the input is [pubkeyA], checkSign(pubkeyA) is true and the function returns true, which is reasonable.

If the input is [pubkeyC], checkSign(pubkeyA) is false, the empty else branch does nothing, and the function returns null rather than true. This also seems reasonable.

The vulnerability is that params is an array, and a user does not have to provide only one parameter.

An attacker can provide the unexpected combination [true, pubkeyC]. After the empty else branch, return params[0] returns true.

There are several basic problems here:

  1. The code does not handle the else branch.
  2. Bitcoin Taproot scripts have no type checking, only opcodes.
  3. The script author did not understand Taproot script usage correctly and overlooked that a witness may submit any number of parameters.

Analysis

This so-called script vulnerability is simply the result of the author writing careless code. The “author” here is not Bitcoin’s creator, but merely a Bitcoin user. Taproot is comparable to an Ethereum smart contract: anyone can write script rules determining how money is controlled and spent. Bitcoin Script is complex and not Turing-complete, so many people overlook that Bitcoin supports custom scripts.

This is clearly not a Bitcoin protocol vulnerability. Bitcoin consensus only executes the script rules correctly; whether the script logic itself is vulnerable is unrelated to the protocol.

In practice, any Bitcoin wallet or ecosystem project relying on Taproot script logic would have its code reviewed by an auditing company. Such a basic error should be extremely rare on mainnet.

Taproot scripts also provide strong privacy. We can know that an address beginning with bc1p is Taproot and that 0xc0 is the current leaf version, but before a UTXO is spent the network cannot see the script’s contents. At the moment it is spent, all the money will probably be transferred away. When a P2TR UTXO is created, the chain stores only the root hash of the tree. Any path that unlocks the root is a valid input, and only during spending does the chain verify the particular leaf and key path. Even if one leaf is revealed, the chain can see only that leaf, not the other leaves beneath the same root.

From the beginning, Bitcoin encouraged using a new address for every transfer, and most reliable wallets do so. This greatly reduces the chance that a vulnerable script can be exploited again.

From both technical and commercial perspectives, vulnerable scripts are exceptionally rare individual cases caused entirely by their authors. The chance of a vulnerable script holding funds on mainnet is very small.

Investigation

Example Address

Could such a vulnerable script really exist on the network, allowing funds to be transferred without a signature?

Starting from bc1p...cn8z, several questions arise.

  1. If this address still held money, how could it be transferred out?

Wallet apps obviously do not provide this function. Bitcoin transactions are also complicated: the originating transaction and output index of each UTXO must be supplied as parameters. This example script, taproot-script-path-demo.mjs, can be run as follows:

TXID='0618d93bc4eef77f4b47c4b4b188011f95c7ccb929e6226df2774b88b5d4693d'VOUT='0'INPUT_SATS='15000'DESTINATION='bc1px6jn77jd4tplp94q46svkuutc53wtn24dk34wxp4dfur6tvez89swvlcmj'FEE_SATS='1000'node outputs/taproot-script-path-demo.mjs \  "$TXID" \  "$VOUT" \  "$INPUT_SATS" \  "$DESTINATION" \  "$FEE_SATS"

If you accidentally send money to bc1p...cn8z, this script can move it without the private key. Be careful: xOnlyKey and payload are hard-coded. Another target address requires different values. What are those values? They become known only after the P2TR output has been spent.

Thus, even if we know an on-chain address has funds and a vulnerable script, we cannot touch the money without the entire tree structure and the xOnlyKey and payload values. From this perspective, Bitcoin assets are still highly secure.

  1. Could the author have sent money to another P2TR output with the same vulnerability and forgotten to withdraw it?

Another example script, audit-taproot-neighborhood.mjs, checks this. The result was no. The author moved all funds from every related address; no such elementary vulnerability remained.

Scanning the Entire Network

This program scans the Bitcoin network for similar script vulnerabilities: tapscript_weak_finder

Its logic is:

  1. Scan every transaction in every block and identify Taproot scripts with version 0xc0.
  2. Use a lightweight interpreter implemented in the program to process witness parameters.
  3. Test whether the script can pass without a signature using three parameter strategies:
    1. Arrange [01, <empty signature>] for zero, one, and two parameters, producing twelve combinations.
    2. Expand the atoms from 01 and <empty signature> to small integers and constants such as 02, 03, true, and false.
    3. For previously revealed witness parameters such as [[data, sigA, sigB]], try variants including [data, "", sigB] and [data, sigA, ""].
  4. Record scripts that require no signature, always return OP_SUCCESS80, or use public-key types not yet defined by the specification.

Scan Results

Of course I will share the results. Running this open-source program will produce the same result and conclusion. I scanned from block 709632, where Taproot activated on mainnet, through block 959701, the latest height at the time.

The program scanned 71,037 blocks, 127,119,410 transactions, and 1,000,061 Taproot addresses. Of these, 427,378 were scripts in which the program recognized no problem, while 12 were potentially vulnerable weak scripts.

Among those 12, eight were weak scripts requiring no signature, one was a non-vulnerable script that always returned OP_SUCCESS80, and three were non-vulnerable scripts containing opcodes unsupported by the scanner’s interpreter.

Result Analysis

Let us examine the potentially weak scripts one by one. The raw, unprocessed output is in result_report.json, from which the addresses, transactions, and scripts below can be reconstructed.

1

The first Taproot address appeared at block 758737: bc1p...2354

It appeared in two abnormal transactions:

  • 00c1...c40e
  • 73be...2a7e

The conclusion first: these were created by highly professional developers to demonstrate Bitcoin mainnet’s BIP342 rules.

The first transaction, 00c1...c40e, contains two witness parameters and was used for testing.

The second, 73be...2a7e, is outrageous: it contains 500,001 witness parameters, while its decoded OP_RETURN text says “you’ll run cln. and you’ll be happy.”

Tapscript normally allows no more than 1,000 elements in the initial stack. The transaction succeeded with 500,001 because BIP342 specifies that if a script contains OP_SUCCESSx, it succeeds regardless of its element count. OP_SUCCESSx consists of opcodes not currently defined but reserved for possible future use, so BIP342 specifies this behavior.

The transaction was clearly demonstrating that situation. Its enormous parameter count cost more than $700 in fees.

2

The next addresses appeared at block 771740:

  • bc1p...648w
  • bc1p...u69a
  • bc1p...n6cl

These three scripts contained OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY, which the scanner did not implement and therefore marked as abnormal. The opcode requires waiting a specified number of blocks before funds can be used and is typical of timelock scripts.

3

At block 775722, the scanner found bc1p...amq6.

This script had a genuine logic vulnerability and allowed funds to move without any signature. It was clearly an Ordinals data wrapper, perhaps created by a developer experimenting with an Ordinals-like protocol. All funds were transferred out at the time, so the address is now empty.

There were several other addresses, not many, mostly Ordinals tests, so I will not analyze each in detail:

  • bc1p...3hu0, block 777335, an Ordinals PNG image.
  • bc1p...xgdr, block 777617, an addition operation without signature verification.
  • bc1p...gq7d, block 777681, a test script that always returns true.
  • bc1p...9x3t, an Ordinals Hello World script.
  • …

Conclusion

I scanned every block and transaction from Taproot activation through the present. A small number of scripts resembling the vulnerability described in How to handle weak scripts? really did appear, but none of those addresses still held funds.

This investigation also suggests two questions:

  1. Are there more complex kinds of script vulnerability on Bitcoin?
  2. Could Ethereum script vulnerabilities be scanned using similar methods?

entry.title: Pitfalls in Building a Polymarket Project
entry.content:
Choosing Wallet Infrastructure

Crypto projects today generally choose Privy.io or Turnkey as their wallet-infrastructure provider. These services integrate registration and login through conventional methods such as email and Google, as well as Web3 methods such as MetaMask or OKX Wallet. More importantly, they solve wallet-security problems by creating embedded wallets for users. Without them, a project must store users’ private keys on its own servers, which is dangerous and imposes a heavy security burden, especially on small and medium-sized teams. Privy and Turnkey hold the private keys in encrypted hardware such as TEEs, while the project accesses and uses the wallets through APIs.

As for choosing between Privy and Turnkey, projects we often examine—including Kreo, PolyCop, and polymtrade—use Privy. They appear on the Polymarket Builder leaderboard, which ranks every project in the Polymarket ecosystem by trading volume. GMGN also uses Privy.

Some projects use Turnkey, including Axiom and Alchemy. We used Turnkey. We initially chose it because its positioning is friendlier to automated trading bots, whereas Privy depends heavily on frontend UI SDKs. Later, we found another major difference: support for Telegram login.

Privy supports Telegram login; Turnkey does not. Why?

Telegram lacks a mature OAuth system like Google’s, so a Telegram account cannot provide Privy or Turnkey with an identity provider in the way an email address or wallet can. Privy simplifies this case: after you log in with Telegram, Privy makes wallet API requests on your behalf. Privy’s backend effectively “is you.” If its servers are compromised, the attacker gains complete wallet authority. Turnkey is more rigid: without an identity provider it will not let you operate the wallet, because its backend refuses to assume that authorization risk for the user.

This is a major difference in scenario support. To use Turnkey while supporting Telegram login, you must build a dedicated Telegram Mini App and invoke it during login.

CLOB V2 Integration

Polymarket’s order system is called CLOB, and actions such as placing orders interact with its API. On April 28, Polymarket officially enabled CLOB V2. For downstream projects like ours, the largest change was replacing contract addresses. Copy Trading, for example, scans on-chain transactions; it previously monitored V1 contracts and had to monitor V2 contracts after migration. A downstream project could also avoid adapting because the old order parameters remained broadly compatible.

CLOB V2 also introduced parameters such as FAK and FOK for market orders. I did not discover their differences until more than a month later. Under V1, the unfilled portion of an order that did not execute immediately was automatically posted as a limit order, while limit orders also required more than five shares. Users therefore encountered strange errors: why did an order require at least five shares, while sometimes the minimum order amount was one dollar? Why did an order sometimes succeed and sometimes fail if the minimum was not fixed? Using FAK avoids this old problem.

Safe Wallet → Deposit Wallet

On May 4, Polymarket announced a new Deposit Wallet, replacing the old Safe wallet. This was a breaking change. Existing users remained compatible, but new wallets—especially API-operated wallets—would use Deposit Wallet, so downstream projects had to adapt.

The timing was delicate because our planned beta launch was May 5. I rushed for two or three consecutive days to adapt to the migration. It was not particularly difficult, but the surprise and launch delay created some pressure.

The only setback was that Polymarket’s migration documentation omitted the new Deposit Wallet implementation address. Creating a wallet through the factory requires an implementation contract parameter, and different implementations produce completely different wallet addresses. The key was not merely which address we used, but which one Polymarket’s Relayer API used, because all wallet operations under the new Deposit Wallet model passed through the official Relayer API. With the old Safe wallet, we could call the on-chain contracts ourselves. This change made the wallet system less decentralized. The correct implementation value had to be read directly from Polymarket’s published SDK. Another pitfall was that different Polymarket SDKs—such as client-sdk and server-sdk, not merely different versions of one SDK—used different implementation addresses. Many developers in Discord encountered this integration problem.

Relayer API

The new Deposit Wallet must use Polymarket’s official Relayer API. After migrating, launching, and running an event, we immediately hit another pitfall: an Unverified Builder API had only 100 requests per day.

See Polymarket’s cunning? First it requires every new user to use Deposit Wallet. Deposit Wallet naturally requires the Relayer API. Then you discover that the API is rate-limited. The old Safe wallet could bypass Polymarket’s API quota by operating directly on-chain; now it cannot.

The Relayer API is used whenever a wallet is created and whenever money is withdrawn, so it is a high-frequency interface.

As a stopgap, Polymarket uses the Builder API to authorize the Relayer API by default, but the Relayer API does not require a particular Builder API. I registered ten accounts, created a Builder API for each, and configured them on the server to ease the quota temporarily. At 100 requests per account per day, ten accounts provided 1,000 daily requests. Verification took two to four weeks, a very long cycle.

We were eventually verified. Our project now appears on the Polymarket Builder leaderboard with Verified status.

Deposit Wallet Upgrade

On July 6, Deposit Wallet caused another problem. We discovered a serious bug: every user registered since July 1 had failed to create a wallet. Because few users reported it, we did not notice for several days. If a new user deposited after registering, the money went to the wrong address.

Why? On July 1, Polymarket directly changed wallet creation to use a beacon-based proxy wallet. It made no announcement and simply changed the API’s behavior, requiring downstream projects to adapt proactively.

We were also at fault because we failed to detect the anomaly promptly and did not add enough protective and defensive measures to the frontend and backend. We reimbursed every affected deposit. Fortunately, the amounts were small.

Combos

Polymarket introduced a feature called Combos for World Cup markets, so we evaluated integrating it. The Combos documentation showed that the API only allowed market makers to submit quotes; it provided no endpoint for ordinary users acting as takers to place orders.

Polymarket began operating the Combos interface on June 4 and appeared to be building it with considerable effort.

Tick Size

On July 10, a user reported a failed order. Investigation showed that the market’s tick size had changed: every World Cup market now supported a precision of 0.0025, or 0.25¢. Previously there were four fixed tick sizes; 0.25¢ was a fifth enum value.

Polymarket had launched this change on July 2, but we did not discover the bug until July 10.

Summary

As you can see, we have continuously followed Polymarket and responded to its feature updates and changes.

During development, we gradually recognized a project trap: building another official website.

If the positioning is “another official website,” the project becomes extremely passive. Polymarket is large and wealthy, its official UI is good, every feature appears there first, and orders are fast on its own servers. Ours can never be faster.

This is awkward. Objectively, making a better experience than the official site is extremely difficult. Polymarket is not a memecoin. Memecoins generally have no official website, wallet, or DEX, while Polymarket has an official site and official solutions. The Builder program was never positioned as an open decentralized protocol that invites everyone to build projects for fun.

On the contrary, Polymarket’s recent updates have become increasingly centralized. Its positioning resembles a centralized exchange such as Binance: the Polymarket API is the Binance API. Building in the Polymarket ecosystem is somewhat like building a Binance trading bot.
